name: Scotch Game: Mieses Variation
summary: Scotch Game, Mieses Variation: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5 Qe7 7.Qe2 Nd5 8.c4 Ba6, Kasparov's sharp modern main line.
intro: The Mieses Variation is the principal theoretical main line of the Scotch Game, reached by 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5 Qe7 7.Qe2 Nd5 8.c4 Ba6. It is an open, sharp, and highly forcing opening in which White stakes out central space with the e5 pawn while Black gains the bishop pair and active piece play in return for doubled c-pawns. Popularised at the top level by Garry Kasparov, it produces concrete, well-mapped positions where accurate move order and precise calculation matter from an early stage.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5 Qe7 Qe2 Nd5 c4 Ba6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The pawn on e5 is the defining feature of the position. It cramps Black, denies the f6-square to Black's pieces, and serves as both a spearhead and a potential target. White supports it with Qe2 and frequently f4, gaining central and kingside space, while c4 immediately challenges the knight that has come to d5. Black's compensation is structural and dynamic: the half-open b-file, the two bishops, and the light-squared bishop on a6 raking the a6-f1 diagonal to pressure the c4 pawn and hinder White's development. The doubled c-pawns look ugly but reinforce Black's grip on d5 and support freeing breaks with ...c5 or ...d6.

Piece activity dominates the middlegame. Black's queen on e7 and bishop on a6 combine to pressure e5 and the light squares, often provoking White to spend time defending. A recurring idea is ...O-O-O, placing the king on the queenside and mobilising the rooks along the central files, though ...g6 and ...Bg7 setups also occur. White typically aims to complete development with Nc3 or Nd2, Be3 or Bg5, and coordinate around the e5 spearhead, sometimes advancing g3 and Bg2 to neutralise the a6-bishop. The struggle centres on whether White can consolidate the extra space or Black's activity and better structure will tell in the long run.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 8.c4 the point of 8...Ba6 is revealed: the bishop attacks the c4 pawn and pins White to defensive measures, so 9.cxd5 is impossible because of 9...Bxe2. White's principal continuation is 9.b3, shoring up c4 and preparing Bb2 and Nd2, when Black develops with ...g6, ...Bg7 and often ...O-O-O for sharp, opposite-side play. The other major branch is 9.Nd2, unpinning the queen and rerouting the knight toward e4 or b3. Black responds with ...g6 and a kingside fianchetto, aiming for ...O-O and pressure on the e5 pawn along the e-file and long diagonal.

Black has flexible setups beyond the immediate ...g6. The plan of ...O-O-O followed by ...Ne7-g6 or ...d6 targets the e5 pawn directly and opens lines for the rooks, at the cost of exposing the king to White's queenside pawn advances. Alternatively, ...Qe6 and ...O-O steer play into calmer channels. For White, a key resource is g3 and Bg2, contesting the long diagonal and blunting the a6-bishop, after which f4-f5 space-gaining plans or a timely trade of the e5-pawn for structural pressure become available. Endgames often favour Black's healthier pawn islands, so White usually keeps pieces on to exploit the space advantage.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Scotch opening dates to the first half of the nineteenth century, taking its name from a correspondence match between London and Edinburgh played in the 1820s. Long overshadowed by the Ruy Lopez, it was revived at the elite level by Garry Kasparov, who employed it as a surprise weapon in his world-championship battles around 1990. The line named after the German master Jacques Mieses, running to 8.c4 Ba6, became the critical modern main line precisely through this revival. Today it is a fully respectable, deeply analysed try for an opening advantage, favoured by players who relish concrete, forcing positions.

keyIdeas: The e5 pawn cramps Black and controls f6, acting as both spearhead and long-term target.
Black's a6-bishop and e7-queen combine to pressure the c4 pawn, e5, and White's light squares.
Doubled c-pawns give Black a firm grip on d5 and support the ...c5 and ...d6 breaks.
...O-O-O with rook pressure on the central files is a thematic, aggressive plan for Black.
White's g3 and Bg2 contest the long diagonal and blunt the a6-bishop.
Precise move order between b3, Nd2, and g3 decides who dominates the centre.

white: Support the e5 spearhead with Qe2 and f4, expanding in the centre and on the kingside.
Play b3 to defend c4 and develop the bishop to b2 on the long diagonal.
Reroute the knight via Nd2-e4 or Nd2-b3 to pressure Black's queenside and centre.
Neutralise the a6-bishop with g3 and Bg2, then push f4-f5 for space.
Keep pieces on the board to exploit the space advantage and avoid favourable endgames for Black.
black: Pressure the c4 pawn and e5 with ...Ba6, ...Qe7, and rook activity.
Castle queenside and attack down the central and e-files against the e5 pawn.
Prepare the freeing breaks ...c5 and ...d6 to undermine White's centre.
Fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7 to reinforce control of the long diagonal.
Exploit the bishop pair and healthier pawn islands, steering toward favourable endgames.
